sections.heading: How to get a reply in three steps
sections.body:
You need three things: the email you got, a few words about what you want to say, and a tone. The reply is ready in about one to three seconds.

1. Open [Email Reply Generator](https://email-reply.lazur.app/) and paste the email you received into the first box.
2. Write what you want to say in your own words, such as: yes to Tuesday, but I need the report by Friday.
3. Pick a tone and start the reply.

Read the reply once, fix any detail that is wrong, and copy it. Step 2 matters most, because the tool can only write what you tell it you want to say. A short, clear line gets a better reply than a vague one.

sections.heading: Choose the tone before you start
sections.body:
The tone sets how the reply sounds. There are four choices.

- **Friendly** for colleagues, and for clients you know well.
- **Professional** for a new contact, a manager, or a formal request.
- **Short and direct** when you need to answer a yes or no question in a few lines.
- **Apologetic** when you are sorry, late, or need to fix a mistake.

If the first reply does not sound like you, run the tool again with a different tone and compare the two versions. Keep the one that sounds like something you would say.

sections.heading: What every reply includes
sections.body:
Every reply starts with a greeting and ends with a sign-off. The tool does not add a subject line, so keep the subject your email app already has, or write your own if the email is new.

The reply is kept as short as the situation allows. If you need more room, say so in what you want to say, for example: explain the three steps in detail. A reply to a simple question should be short. A reply to a complaint, or to a request with several parts, may need more, and the more you tell the tool, the more the reply can cover.

Send only what you would stand behind if you had written every word yourself. For legal, medical or money decisions, treat the reply as a draft and get the right advice before you send it.

pages.description: Good email greetings by situation: Dear with a name for formal email, Hi with a name for most work email, and Hi everyone for a group. Examples inside.
pages.h1: What are good greetings for emails
pages.claim: Use Dear with a name for formal email, Hi with a name for most work email, and Hi everyone for a group. Avoid Hey in job applications and first contact. Or let the reply tool write the greeting for you.

sections.heading: Good greetings by situation
sections.body:
The right greeting depends on how well you know the person and how formal the email is.

For formal email, when you know the name:

- Dear Ms. Taylor,
- Dear Dr. Patel,
- Dear Alex Morgan,

For formal email, when you know the job but not the name, use a role such as Dear Hiring Manager or Dear Customer Support Team.

For everyday work email:

- Hi Alex,
- Hello Jordan, for someone you have just met
- Hi Alex and Sam, for two people
- Hi everyone or Hello team, for a group

Hi with a first name is the most common choice in work email. It is friendly without being too casual.

sections.heading: Dear with a name, or a role
sections.body:
Use Dear with a name when you know the name and the right title. Use a role, like Dear Hiring Manager, when you know the job but not the person. Use the name the person uses for themselves, and do not shorten Joseph to Joe unless he does.

Mr. and Ms. go with last names, not first names. Write Dear Ms. Smith, not Dear Ms. Anna. Put a comma after the greeting in business email.

sections.heading: Greetings to avoid
sections.body:
Some greetings can make a reader feel ignored or unsure of you.

- Hey, for job applications, cold outreach, and first contact with a client.
- Dear Sir or Madam, when you know anything about the person. It is traditional but impersonal.
- A title with a first name, such as Dear Mr. Anna.

If you are not sure, use Hi or Hello with the name. They fit most work email and suit a first message better than Hey.

sections.heading: Greetings in a long thread
sections.body: After the first message or two, you can switch from Dear to Hi and the name, or drop the greeting in a fast back-and-forth. Keep the greeting you started with when the topic is serious, such as a complaint, a contract, or a problem that needs a clear record.

Every reply from this tool starts with a greeting and ends with a sign-off. Paste the email you got, say what you want to say, and pick a tone: Friendly for people you know, Professional for formal email, Short and direct for quick answers, and Apologetic when you need to say sorry.

Read the greeting first and check the name before you send. The tool is free, with 3 runs a day and no account. You get 3 more after you leave an email address. Start at [Email Reply Generator](https://email-reply.lazur.app/).

If you write email all day, Lazur does this in any app on your Mac. Lazur is a Mac app (Windows is coming): hold two keys and talk, and it types, answers or does the task in whatever app you are in.

faq.q: What is a good greeting for a formal email?
faq.a: For a formal email, use Dear with the person's title and last name, such as Dear Ms. Taylor or Dear Dr. Patel. If you do not know the name, use a role like Dear Hiring Manager. Dear Sir or Madam is traditional, but use it only when you know nothing about the recipient.

faq.q: What is another word for greetings?
faq.a: Greetings can also be called salutations. In an email, the greeting is the first line, such as Hi Alex or Dear Ms. Smith, and the sign-off is the last line, such as Best regards. Both are part of the same email, so choose them together.

faq.q: What's a funny way to start an email?
faq.a: Keep it light only with someone you know well, such as a close colleague or friend. Hi, stranger or Hello, sunshine can work in that case. Avoid jokes with a client, a manager, or anyone you have not met, because they can read as careless. If you are not sure, use Hi and the name.

faq.q: What are common greeting words in English?
faq.a: Common greetings include Dear, Hi, Hello, Good morning, and Hi everyone. Dear is the most formal, Hi is the most common in work email, and Hello sits between them. Use Good morning or Good afternoon only when the time of day fits the reader.
